help.text: The Helm station lets you steer the ship. The weapons station controls your beams and your torpedoes. The engineering station lets you control the energy allocation and the DamCon teams. The science station is the eyes of the ship, and shows a big map of the sector. The comms station has a text scroll, and is the voice of the ship.

Since the Helm is busy half the time with tricky maneuvering, responsibility for changing the main screen view will likely fall to the Weapons officer, who has less micromanaging to do. Be ready to jump on orders to change views quickly.

As the Weapons officer, keep an eye on the enemy ship's shields, especially which hemisphere is weaker. When you are ordered to fire torpedoes (especially at will), keep an eye on the relative position of the Artemis' fore relative to the enemy so that you can place those torpedo hits on their weaker hemisphere.

As the Weapons officer, remember shields significantly increase energy consumption. Be prepared to drop shields if the captain calls for a high warp. By the same token, be prepared to quickly raise shields if the Artemis is coming within range of an enemy ship's weapons.

The Weapons officer should coordinate with Helm to stay on a single shield facing of the enemy. Depending on the skill of your pilot, he/she may start to drift into the wrong (That is to say, less damaged) shield facing, and having WEAP request a course change to compensate is sometimes helpful, especially if the captain is busy issuing other commands.
WEAP needs to make sure that SCI is feeding him the weakest (lowest) shield frequency of the current enemy target.

Engineering can adjust power to ship systems. For beams, more power means more shots per second. For tubes, more power means a faster reload speed. For shields, more power means you can take more hits to the shields before they go down. For impulse and warp, more power means more sheer speed. For maneuver, more power means faster turning. No power in tactical means that you lose sensors.
Don't play Science or Comms if you can't speak up! These stations have lots of information that everyone else needs, and your job is to tell them.
The steering of the ship can be done with the drag bars, OR the arrow keys, OR the WASD keys, or a USB joystick.

Helm officer: Your maneuvering bar is not an on/off switch. When you stop adjusting it, you will not automatically level out and fly straight, you will continue turning at whatever rate you left it at.
Artemis is more maneuverable than the enemy ships and roughly twice as fast at full impulse, so be prepared to drop your impulse speed to maintain the ideal rotation relative to the enemy.

A good Helms officer will make use of Artemis's speed advantage. The enemies move at roughly half impulse. You can easily use your warp drive to get in their weapons' blind spot and come about at low impulse before they can. Then you simply match their speed and direction keeping them in your sights. Of course it gets more complicated when there are more than one enemy ship, but the same basic premise applies. Just use your warp whenever you are about to get caught in the crossfire.

Helm officer: Do NOT stay at one speed in combat. You make tighter turns at lower speeds, and wider turns at higher speeds, so depending on where you are trying to go, and when you want to be there, you adjust your speed to fit your goal.
The comms station has a 'RED ALERT' button which is entirely cosmetic. However, if your crew is falling asleep, your captain can ask for a red alert, and you can give it to her.
The comms station can taunt enemies, but there are three different taunts, and each enemy will respond to each taunt only once (at most), so don't waste your taunts.
On the Science console, enemies can be scanned more than once, to reveal more information about them.

A good captain understands the line between micromanaging and leadership. A captain shouldn't be shouting "now go more left, no more right" but "Helm, keep us behind O21 and her rear shields in target".

A good captain doesn't keep the main screen for herself; she understands that every crew member needs to see the main screen too. Every crew member knows that the captain will lean over them and look at their screen, too. Which is why a good captain wears deodorant. :)

A good captain keeps communicating with Engineering. The engineer has the most power over the ship and the least tactical information about the situation. The captain should coordinate the execution of tasks like firing torpedoes with engineering closely to maximise their effect.

As Captain, don't let your engineer take down *all* power from warp drive, or either shield, unless you directly order her to. There's a good chance she'll be slow to put those systems back online when it's imperative that they are working. On this point, don't fall prey to overly dramatic speech - don't say 'full power to the forward shield' unless you actually mean it - you'll only have yourself to blame when there's no power left for beams or torpedoes
On the Weapons console, two small buttons on the right allow you to trade Mark 1 torpedoes for energy, and vice versa.

Oh no! You've run out of energy far from a base! 1) The weapons officer can trade a homing torpedo for energy. Does she have one? 2) the ship WILL recover energy slowly, if the engineer shuts down every system (this works better at lower difficulty levels). 3) space anomalies can be found by the Science officer. If you can reach one, you'll recover energy from it.

The ship has a self-destruct sequence. -(helm/weapons) lower shields -(helm) stop dead -(engineer) reduce all systems power to zero. -(engineer) increase power to warp, to cause an overload. On overload, your ship flares up like an exploding sun!
